newsitem.title: USA: Merck exits crop protection, focuses on drugs.
newsitem.headline: Merck exits crop protection, focuses on drugs.

text.p: Merck & Co's sale of its agricultural chemical business to Novartis AG for a tidy $910 million could be its last big divestiture, as it concentrates on its lucrative drug-making business.

Analysts said Merck received a substantial price for a business some criticised as cyclical and low-profit, adding the company was now free to grow through internal drug development, acquisitions and alliances.

"Though it's not a big deal by Merck standards, it gets the company more focused on the high growth, high margin business of human pharmaceuticals," David Saks, an equity analyst with Gruntal & Co said.
Merck shares were trading off 5/8 at 92 points.
"They don't really have anything else left to divest," Cynthia Beach, an analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattision said.
It could also boost margins and the bottom line slightly, although most analysts said even a $910 million sale would not have much effect on Merck's massive balance sheet.

"It's a good move and helps them focus on human and animal pharmaceuticals," said Michael Binz, an analyst with Edward Jones. "It might help the bottom line a little next year, though any benefit would be negligible."
The crop protection business, based in Woodbridge, N.J., had sales of about $200 million in 1996, Merck said.
Merck said the over the past four years, the operation posted annualized gross profit growth of 12 percent and operating income growth of 13 percent.
While the unit had not been a drag Merck's recent results, Saks said: "The crop protection business is cyclical, irregular pattern and low profit."
In contrast, its pharmaceutical business was growing between 15 and 20 percent annually with margins of between 30 and 40 percent, he sai.
The unit dealt in niche crop protection markets, making abamectin, an insecticide marketed under the trade marks of Agri-mek and Vertimic and used on fruits and vegetables.
Avid, another of the unit's insecticides, was used on so-called "ornamentals," like roses, other flowering plants while its Zephyr insecticide was used on cotton, Merck said.
The operation also made fungicides, used after the crop harvested, called thiabendazole and marketed as Mertect.

In December 1996, Merck announced plans to combine its animal health and poultry genetics businesses into a new joint venture with a unit of France's Rhone-Poulenc SA. It said then it would try to sell the crop protection unit.

Merck said the sale was part of a strategy to focus on its core human and animal health business. A Merck spokesman said Novartis made what the company considered was the best offer despite a nubmer of other "financially aggressive" bidders.

Novartis said it would buy the unit because it had "a strong position in the high-value acaricide/insectide and post-harvest fungicide markets." These referred to products which protected crops against mites, insects and fungi.
The sale liberated money Merck could use elsewhere to corner a greater share of the global drug market, Brian Eisenbarth, an analyst at Collins & Co, said.
"It gets rid of business not really related to the company's core businesses," Eisenbarth said. "Company resources can now be allocated to areas of high growth like drug developement."
((--New York newsdesk 212-859-1737))
